newsitem.title: USA: Five years after riots - healing in Los Angeles?.
newsitem.headline: Five years after riots - healing in Los Angeles?.

text.p: Five years ago, America's second largest city was burning.
A jury's acquittal of white policemen for beating a black man fanned the flames of racial mistrust and rage, devastating large areas of the city and scarring its people.

There were searing images -- looters leaping through shattered shop windows to carry off TV's and other appliances; Korean store-owners waving guns to protect shops; black youths swaggering over the prone body of white truck driver Reginald Denny as they took turns smashing bricks into his head.

Denny lived, but more than 50 people died in the worst civil unrest in the United States this century. The state National Guard and federal troops were called out to help quell the unrest, which also spread to a dozen other cities.
"Everyone was fleeing the city ... I saw a dozen columns of smoke. It was like Beirut," recalled Elaine Burn, who was working in the Koreatown section the day the riots erupted.

"It was the most frightening experience of my life," she said, adding that she stayed up all night, scared to sleep with the sounds of gunfire and violence audible down the street from her apartment bulding.

There are few events planned for Tuesday -- the anniversary of the start of the riots -- but empty lots in predominantly black South-Central Los Angeles bear stark testimony to the three days of violence and the still simmering anger.

"We're all scratching like chickens looking for worms, but there aren't so many worms," said South-Central resident Joseph Long. "People of colour are bitter and angry, because now they only get a bone thrown at them now and then."
"Los Angeles still suffers from major wounds and a continuing racial divide," said John Mack, local president of the Urban League, a predominantly black civil rights group.

Few Angelenos believe it has healed from the April 29-May 1, 1992, riots in a city that likes to think of itself as America's new melting pot. Barely 40 percent of the 3.5 million population is white, while a huge Hispanic community makes up more than 30 percent and various Asian groups outnumber the roughly 10 percent blacks.
The street violence and police response to it resulted in the resignation of police chief Darryl Gates, thought by many minorites to symbolise institutionalized racial intolerance.

He was replaced by a black chief, Willie Williams. But this month the city did not renew Williams' five-year contract, saying it was unhappy with his management style and lack of confidence in him by officers on the streets.

Several high-profile criminal cases too have underscored the racial tension under the surface here -- none more so than that of black ex-football star O.J. Simpson. When he was acquitted in 1995 of murdering his white wife, the police force was on tactical alert, a sign the city fathers feared an explosion of anti-white violence if he had been convicted.

The trigger of the 1992 riots was the acquittal of four white officers in the videotaped beating of black motorist Rodney King after a car chase. Two of the officers were subsequently jailed on federal charges but the police are viewed with suspicion by most civil rights groups.
"If you look at the history of civil disturbances, almost all relate to police brutality," said Mack. "In many ways, the ball is in the court of the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department)."
"Recovery is extremely difficult in part because of continued events that expose the racial bigotry and intolerance," Mack said.

Long's voice from the street was more blunt: "A revolution is coming. We're sitting on a powder keg and we're gonna blow. I hope I'm not around when it happens," he told a local newspaper, L.A. Weekly.

Risa Mandelberg, who lives in the San Fernando Valley suburbs, expressed continuing fear: "Prior to the riots, L.A. had an optimistic view of itself as a city pf many races, but the riots showed this was not the case. It was very scary. I am more wary now."
"It was more devastating for the city than the earthquake (of January 1994) and I felt more personally threatened than by the quake," said Mandelberg, who is white.

Alexander Moore, a professor of anthropolgy at the University of Southern California, warned that the twin evils of unemployment and lack of education among the poor could lead to more riots like the ones in South-Central in 1992 and the 1965 civil rights uprising in nearby Watts.
"In large cities, unemployment and discontent can lead to riots. I will not be surprised if, unless there are real changes, we'll have them again in 20 years."

His colleague, Eric Schockman, of USC's Centre for Multiethnic and Transnational Studies, agreed. "We have played lip service after '92. Private industry promised jobs and it has not happened," he said, referring to the 1992 events as "multi-ethnic bread riots."
But he predicted a peaceful "civic revolution at the polls," as a result of the new racial awareness and a rush of recent immigrants to register as voters.
